title: Conducting a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topics 3.12 and 3.13 Conducting a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
intro: After this lesson you can name the two-sample $z$ test, state hypotheses about $p_1-p_2$, check conditions with the combined proportion, compute the $z$ statistic and p-value, and write a conclusion in context.

moments.title: When a test is needed
moments.text: A claim about two population proportions plus the words "is there evidence".

moments.title: Three situations
moments.text: Two age groups and brand A, reminder emails and on-time assignments, exercise and stress.

moments.title: Compare with a difference
moments.text: Samples vary, so a 9% difference in samples is only evidence, not proof.

moments.title: Sampling distribution centered at zero
moments.text: Built assuming no difference between the population proportions.

moments.title: Name and parameter together
moments.text: "A two-sample $z$ test for $p_1-p_2$." Then define $p_1$ and $p_2$ in context.

moments.title: Hypotheses use $p$, not $\hat p$
moments.text: They describe the populations, not the samples.

moments.title: Conditions
moments.text: Random sampling or random assignment, 10% for each sample (sampling only), and large counts.

moments.title: Use the combined proportion
moments.text: $\hat p_c=\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}$, because $H_0$ says the proportions are equal.

moments.title: Large counts with $\hat p_c$
moments.text: Check $n_1\hat p_c$, $n_1(1-\hat p_c)$, $n_2\hat p_c$ and $n_2(1-\hat p_c)$ are at least 10.

moments.title: p-value
moments.text: The probability of a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than observed, assuming $H_0$ is true.

moments.title: Two-sided tests double the tail
moments.text: Use both tails when $H_a$ is $p_1\ne p_2$.

moments.title: Compare p-value to $\alpha$
moments.text: Then conclude about the alternative in context, with careful wording.

moments.title: Say "evidence", never "proved"
moments.text: Never say the null is true or false.

moments.title: Younger and older customers, brand A
moments.text: 96/210 against 88/240: $z=1.948$, p-value $0.0515$. Fail to reject at 0.05.

moments.title: Experiments use random assignment
moments.text: Do not check the 10% condition for a randomized experiment.

cards.name: Different
cards.text: "Is there a difference?" gives $H_a: p_1\ne p_2$ and a two-sided test.

cells: Younger and older customers differ in preferring brand A
Reminder emails raise the on-time proportion
Adults who exercise report high stress less often
A new teaching method improves pass rate (new minus old)
A policy changes support (after minus before, independent samples)
Region 1 has a lower rate than region 2

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The null hypothesis always says there is no difference. The alternative follows the direction in the question, with the proportions defined in context before you use them.

sections.title: Carry out a two-sample z test

questions.obj: Carry out a two-sided two-sample z test
questions.q: 96 of 210 randomly selected younger customers and 88 of 240 randomly selected older customers prefer brand A. Do the data provide convincing evidence of a difference between the proportion of younger customers and the proportion of older customers who prefer brand A? Use $\alpha=0.05$.

steps.t: Parameter and Name: name the test and define the parameters.

work.text: This is a two-sample $z$ test for $p_Y-p_O$, where $p_Y$ is the proportion of all younger customers who prefer brand A and $p_O$ is the proportion of all older customers who prefer brand A.

steps.t: Hypotheses: write $H_0$ and $H_a$ in the direction asked.

work.text: The question asks about a difference, so the alternative is two-sided.

steps.t: Assumptions: check the samples, the 10% condition, and the counts using $\hat p_c$.

work.text: Both samples are random, and each is less than 10% of its population. The four expected counts are all at least 10, using the combined proportion.

steps.t: Test statistic: divide the difference in sample proportions by the standard error.

work.text: The difference is younger minus older, and the standard error uses $\hat p_c$.

steps.t: p-value: find the area beyond the test statistic and double it.

work.text: The area is doubled because the test is two-sided.

steps.t: Conclusion: compare the p-value with $\alpha$ and answer in context.

work.text: The p-value is greater than $\alpha$, so we fail to reject $H_0$.

questions.answer: The p-value of 0.0515 is greater than 0.05, so we fail to reject $H_0$. There is not convincing evidence of a difference between the proportion of younger customers and the proportion of older customers who prefer brand A.

questions.obj: Carry out a one-sided two-sample z test for an experiment
questions.q: A professor randomly assigned 350 students to two groups of 175. In the group that got reminder emails, 146 students turned in their homework on time. In the group that did not, 126 did. Do the data provide convincing evidence that reminder emails increase the proportion of students who turn in homework on time? Use $\alpha=0.05$.

steps.t: Parameter and Name: name the test and define the parameters.

work.text: This is a two-sample $z$ test for $p_E-p_N$, where $p_E$ is the proportion of students like these who would turn in homework on time with reminder emails and $p_N$ is the proportion without them.

steps.t: Hypotheses: write $H_0$ and $H_a$ in the direction asked.

work.text: The professor wants evidence that emails increase the proportion, so the alternative is one-sided.

steps.t: Assumptions: check random assignment and the counts using $\hat p_c$.

work.text: The students were randomly assigned, so the 10% condition is not checked. The four expected counts are all at least 10, using the combined proportion.

steps.t: Test statistic: divide the difference in sample proportions by the standard error.

work.text: The difference is email group minus no-email group, matching the order in $H_a$.

steps.t: p-value: find the area beyond the test statistic.

work.text: Only the upper tail counts because the test is one-sided.

steps.t: Conclusion: compare the p-value with $\alpha$ and answer in context.

work.text: The p-value is less than $\alpha$, so we reject $H_0$.

questions.answer: The p-value of 0.0051 is less than 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence that the proportion of students like these who turn in homework on time is greater with reminder emails than without them.

traps.title: Conclusion about the alternative, in context
traps.weak: We reject the null because the p-value is small.
traps.better: The p-value of 0.0051 is less than $\alpha=0.05$, so we reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence that the proportion of students similar to those in the study who submit assignments on time is greater when they receive reminder emails than when they do not.

traps.title: Failing to reject is not accepting the null
traps.weak: There is no difference between younger and older customers.
traps.better: The p-value of 0.0515 is greater than 0.05, so we fail to reject $H_0$. There is not convincing evidence of a difference between the proportion of younger customers and the proportion of older customers who prefer brand A.

traps.title: Hats in the hypotheses
traps.better: $H_0: p_1=p_2$, with $p_1$ and $p_2$ defined as the population proportions in context.

traps.title: Checking counts with separate proportions
traps.weak: Both samples have at least 10 successes and failures using $\hat p_1$ and $\hat p_2$.
traps.better: Because $H_0$ says the proportions are equal, check counts with the combined proportion, for example $210(0.409)$ and $210(1-0.409)$.

traps.title: Forgetting to double the tail
traps.weak: For $H_a: p_1\ne p_2$ the p-value is the one-tail area.
traps.better: For a two-sided alternative, double the one-tail area, or ask the calculator for both tails.

questions.stem: A randomized experiment assigns 120 volunteers to an app and 130 to a paper log. Which condition is NOT checked for a two-sample $z$ test?
opts: Independence of the two groups through the design
Large counts using the combined proportion
why: Random assignment makes the groups independent.
Correct. There is no random sample from a population, so the 10% condition is not checked.

questions.stem: In group 1, 54 of 120 succeed. In group 2, 38 of 130 succeed. What is $\hat p_c$?
why: This averages the two proportions, ignoring the different sample sizes.
This is the difference of the sample proportions.

questions.stem: For $H_a: p_1\ne p_2$ with $z=1.80$, what is the p-value?
why: This is not a tail area.
Correct. A two-sided alternative doubles the tail area.

questions.stem: A two-sample test gives p-value 0.031 at $\alpha=0.05$. Which conclusion is best?
opts: There is convincing evidence that the population proportions differ.
The null hypothesis is proved false.
There is a 3.1% chance the null is true.
why: Correct. The p-value is below 0.05, so reject $H_0$ and conclude in context about the alternative.
A test never proves the null false.
The p-value is a probability computed assuming $H_0$ is true.
A p-value this small does not support equality.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A researcher randomly assigned 120 volunteers to use a walking app and 130 volunteers to keep a paper log. After a month, 54 of the app users and 38 of the paper-log users met their step goal. Do the data provide convincing evidence that the proportion who meet the goal is greater with the app? Use $\alpha=0.05$.
parts: (a) State the name of the test and the hypotheses with the parameters defined.
(c) Calculate the test statistic and p-value.
sample: (a) A two-sample $z$ test for $p_A-p_L$, where $p_A$ is the proportion of volunteers like these who would meet their step goal using the app and $p_L$ is the proportion using the paper log. $H_0: p_A=p_L$; $H_a: p_A>p_L$.

(d) The p-value $0.0049$ is less than 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence that the proportion of volunteers like these who meet their step goal is greater with the app than with the paper log.
checklist: (a) Two-sample z test, parameters defined in context
(b) Four counts with the combined proportion
